claim: The central complex (CX) of the adult Drosophila melanogaster brain consists of approximately 2800 cells.
source: The central complex (CX) of the adult Drosophila melanogaster brain consists of approximately 2800 cells that have been divided into 257 cell types based on morphology and connectivity (Scheffer et al., 2020; Hulse et al., 2021; Wolff et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published connectome studies (Scheffer et al., 2020; Hulse et al., 2021; Wolff et al., 2015).

claim: The central complex cells have been divided into 257 cell types based on morphology and connectivity.
source: The central complex (CX) of the adult Drosophila melanogaster brain consists of approximately 2800 cells that have been divided into 257 cell types based on morphology and connectivity (Scheffer et al., 2020; Hulse et al., 2021; Wolff et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published connectome studies (Scheffer et al., 2020; Hulse et al., 2021; Wolff et al., 2015).

claim: The CX plays a key role in the flow of information between sensory inputs and motor outputs.
source: The CX plays a key role in the flow of information between sensory inputs and motor outputs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about CX function.

claim: The CX is particularly important in orientation and navigation.
source: It is particularly important in orientation and navigation, and much progress has been made in defining the cell types and circuits involved in these behaviors (reviewed in Fisher, 2022; Green and Maimon, 2018; Pfeiffer, 2022; Turner-Evans and Jayaraman, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple review articles (Fisher, 2022; Green and Maimon, 2018; Pfeiffer, 2022; Turner-Evans and Jayaraman, 2016).

claim: The CX appears to participate in sleep and/or activity regulation.
source: The CX also appears to participate in sleep and/or activity regulation (reviewed in Dubowy and Sehgal, 2017; Shafer and Keene, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to review articles (Dubowy and Sehgal, 2017; Shafer and Keene, 2021).

claim: The CX is one of the most peptidergic brain areas.
source: This is particularly relevant for the CX, which is one of the most peptidergic brain areas (Kahsai and Winther, 2011; Nässel and Zandawala, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Kahsai and Winther, 2011; Nässel and Zandawala, 2019).

claim: The authors generated split-GAL4 driver lines that express in individual or small subsets of about half of CX cell types.
source: We generated and characterized split-GAL4 driver lines that express in individual or small subsets of about half of CX cell types.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by the data presented in Figures 2 and Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: About half of the neuropeptides examined were expressed in only a few cells.
source: About half of the neuropeptides we examined were expressed in only a few cells, while the rest were expressed in dozens to hundreds of cells.
evidence: This is supported by the EASI-FISH data shown in Figures 5-7.

claim: About half of the neuropeptides examined were expressed in dozens to hundreds of cells.
source: About half of the neuropeptides we examined were expressed in only a few cells, while the rest were expressed in dozens to hundreds of cells.
evidence: This is supported by the EASI-FISH data shown in Figures 5-7.

claim: Neuropeptide receptors were expressed more broadly and at lower levels than neuropeptides.
source: Neuropeptide receptors were expressed more broadly and at lower levels.
evidence: This is supported by the EASI-FISH data shown in Figure 7.

claim: 51 of the 85 CX cell types examined expressed at least one neuropeptide.
source: Using our GAL4 drivers to mark individual cell types, we found that 51 of the 85 CX cell types we examined expressed at least one neuropeptide and 21 expressed multiple neuropeptides.
evidence: This is supported by the data summarized in Figure 9.

claim: 21 of the 85 CX cell types examined expressed multiple neuropeptides.
source: Using our GAL4 drivers to mark individual cell types, we found that 51 of the 85 CX cell types we examined expressed at least one neuropeptide and 21 expressed multiple neuropeptides.
evidence: This is supported by the data summarized in Figure 9.

claim: All neuropeptide-expressing CX cell types co-expressed a small molecule neurotransmitter.
source: Surprisingly, all co-expressed a small molecule neurotransmitter.
evidence: This is supported by the data summarized in Figure 9.

claim: The authors generated 52 new split-GAL4 lines with strong GAL4 expression largely limited to the cell type of interest.
source: Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplements 1–4 show the expression of 52 new split-GAL4 lines with strong GAL4 expression that is largely limited to the cell type of interest.
evidence: This is supported by the images shown in Figure 2 and supplementary figures.

claim: The authors generated high-quality lines for nearly one-third of CX cell types defined by connectome analysis.
source: Together with the other lines generated in this study and our previous work, we generated high-quality lines for nearly one-third of CX cell types that were defined by analysis of the connectome (Hulse et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a summary of the split-GAL4 line generation effort, with reference to the connectome study (Hulse et al., 2021).

claim: The authors generated lines covering more than three quarters of CX cell types in total.
source: We also generated lines of lesser quality for other cell types that in total bring overall coverage to more than three quarters of CX cell types.
evidence: This is a summary of the total coverage achieved by the split-GAL4 line generation effort.

claim: PFG neurons use tyramine as a neurotransmitter.
source: PFG cell bodies show expression of Tdc2 but not Tbh indicating that the PFG neurons use tyramine as a neurotransmitter.
evidence: This is supported by EASI-FISH data shown in Figure 4A-D demonstrating Tdc2 expression but not Tbh expression.

claim: FB4K neurons co-express acetylcholine and glutamate.
source: Here, the FB tangential neuron FB4K expresses RNAs suggesting it can release both acetylcholine and glutamate.
evidence: This is supported by EASI-FISH data shown in Figure 4E-H demonstrating expression of ChAT, VAChT, and vGlut.

claim: Cases of co-transmission using two fast-acting neurotransmitters are rare in Drosophila.
source: Cases of co-transmission using two fast-acting neurotransmitters have been described in many organisms (reviewed in Svensson et al., 2018) including Drosophila, but are rare and may be post-transcriptionally regulated (Chen et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review (Svensson et al., 2018) and research (Chen et al., 2023) articles.

claim: Every cell type that expressed a neuropeptide also expressed a small molecule neurotransmitter.
source: Second, every cell type that expressed a neuropeptide also expressed a small molecule neurotransmitter (see Nässel, 2018 for a discussion of other cases of co-expression).
evidence: This is supported by the data summarized in Figure 9.

claim: Co-transmission of two small molecule, fast-acting transmitters occurs but is rare in CX cell types.
source: Third, co-transmission of two small molecule, fast-acting transmitters does occur but is rare.
evidence: This is supported by the data summarized in Figure 9.

claim: Nine of ten cell types expressing the serotonin transporter also express another small transmitter.
source: Conversely, co-transmission of a fast-acting transmitter and a modulatory transmitter such as serotonin is common: nine of ten cell types expressing the serotonin transporter also express another small transmitter, most often glutamate or acetylcholine.
evidence: This is supported by the data summarized in Figure 9.

claim: Octopamine is often co-expressed with glutamate.
source: Octopamine is often, but not always, co-expressed with glutamate (see also Sherer et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the data summarized in Figure 9 and a citation to Sherer et al., 2020.

claim: hDeltaF is strongly wake promoting when activated.
source: For example, hDeltaF was found to be strongly wake promoting (Figure 10).
evidence: This is supported by thermogenetic and optogenetic activation data shown in Figure 10.

claim: PEN_b likely plays a role in sleep/activity regulation.
source: We also identified PEN_b (Figure 10—figure supplement 1), PFGs (Figure 10—figure supplement 2), EL (Figure 10—figure supplement 3), and hDeltaK (Figure 10—figure supplement 4) as likely to play a role.
evidence: This is supported by thermogenetic and optogenetic activation data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: PFGs likely play a role in sleep/activity regulation.
source: We also identified PEN_b (Figure 10—figure supplement 1), PFGs (Figure 10—figure supplement 2), EL (Figure 10—figure supplement 3), and hDeltaK (Figure 10—figure supplement 4) as likely to play a role.
evidence: This is supported by thermogenetic and optogenetic activation data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 2.

claim: EL likely plays a role in sleep/activity regulation.
source: We also identified PEN_b (Figure 10—figure supplement 1), PFGs (Figure 10—figure supplement 2), EL (Figure 10—figure supplement 3), and hDeltaK (Figure 10—figure supplement 4) as likely to play a role.
evidence: This is supported by thermogenetic and optogenetic activation data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 3.

claim: hDeltaK likely plays a role in sleep/activity regulation.
source: We also identified PEN_b (Figure 10—figure supplement 1), PFGs (Figure 10—figure supplement 2), EL (Figure 10—figure supplement 3), and hDeltaK (Figure 10—figure supplement 4) as likely to play a role.
evidence: This is supported by thermogenetic and optogenetic activation data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 4.

claim: SMP368 is strongly wake promoting when activated.
source: Figure 11 (SMP368) and Figure 11—figure supplement 1 (SMP531) present two such cases of strongly wake promoting cell types.
evidence: This is supported by thermogenetic and optogenetic activation data shown in Figure 11.

claim: SMP531 is strongly wake promoting when activated.
source: Figure 11 (SMP368) and Figure 11—figure supplement 1 (SMP531) present two such cases of strongly wake promoting cell types.
evidence: This is supported by thermogenetic and optogenetic activation data shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 1.

claim: SMP368 connects central clock outputs to the CX.
source: SMP368 connects central clock outputs to the CX (see Figure 12, Figure 12—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by connectivity data shown in Figure 12 and Figure 12—figure supplement 1.

claim: SMP531 is part of a potential pathway from clock outputs to the CX.
source: SMP531 is part of a potential pathway from clock outputs to the CX (see Figure 12—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by connectivity data shown in Figure 12—figure supplement 1.

claim: ER5 cells express receptors for both PDF and Dh44.
source: Our RNA profiling of ER5 cells (Figure 9—figure supplement 1), which are known to be regulators of sleep and sleep homeostasis (Liu et al., 2016), revealed expression of receptors for both PDF and Dh44.
evidence: This is supported by RNA profiling data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: ER5 cells are regulators of sleep and sleep homeostasis.
source: Our RNA profiling of ER5 cells (Figure 9—figure supplement 1), which are known to be regulators of sleep and sleep homeostasis (Liu et al., 2016), revealed expression of receptors for both PDF and Dh44.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2016.

claim: The presence of the PDF receptor in ER5 cells was suggested by prior work.
source: The presence of the PDF receptor in ER5 cells was suggested by prior work (Im and Taghert, 2010; Parisky et al., 2008; Pírez et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Im and Taghert, 2010; Parisky et al., 2008; Pírez et al., 2013).

claim: ER5 cells make Dh31.
source: We confirmed these observations and showed that ER5 cells make Dh31 (Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by EASI-FISH data shown in Video 1.

claim: Dh44 has been implicated as a clock output that regulates locomotor activity rhythms.
source: Dh44 has been implicated as a clock output that regulates locomotor activity rhythms (Barber et al., 2021; Cavanaugh et al., 2014) and the DH44R1 receptor has been shown to function in sleep regulation in non-CX cells (King et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies (Barber et al., 2021; Cavanaugh et al., 2014).

claim: The DH44R1 receptor has been shown to function in sleep regulation in non-CX cells.
source: Dh44 has been implicated as a clock output that regulates locomotor activity rhythms (Barber et al., 2021; Cavanaugh et al., 2014) and the DH44R1 receptor has been shown to function in sleep regulation in non-CX cells (King et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to King et al., 2017.

claim: The presence of the Dh44R2 receptor in the ellipsoid body was unexpected.
source: However, the presence of the Dh44R2 receptor in the ellipsoid body (EB) was unexpected.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the authors based on their EASI-FISH data.

claim: Dh31 is expressed by many cells in the fly brain including DN1s.
source: Dh31 is expressed by many cells in the fly brain (see Figure 6F) including DN1s (Kunst et al., 2014) and has been shown to play a role in sleep regulation; the cellular targets of Dh31 released from ER5 are unknown, however previous work (Goda et al., 2016; Mertens et al., 2005; Shafer et al., 2008) has shown that Dh31 can activate the PDF receptor raising the possibility of autocrine signaling.
evidence: This is supported by EASI-FISH data shown in Figure 6F and citations to published studies (Kunst et al., 2014).

claim: Dh31 has been shown to play a role in sleep regulation.
source: Dh31 is expressed by many cells in the fly brain (see Figure 6F) including DN1s (Kunst et al., 2014) and has been shown to play a role in sleep regulation; the cellular targets of Dh31 released from ER5 are unknown, however previous work (Goda et al., 2016; Mertens et al., 2005; Shafer et al., 2008) has shown that Dh31 can activate the PDF receptor raising the possibility of autocrine signaling.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Dh31 can activate the PDF receptor.
source: Dh31 is expressed by many cells in the fly brain (see Figure 6F) including DN1s (Kunst et al., 2014) and has been shown to play a role in sleep regulation; the cellular targets of Dh31 released from ER5 are unknown, however previous work (Goda et al., 2016; Mertens et al., 2005; Shafer et al., 2008) has shown that Dh31 can activate the PDF receptor raising the possibility of autocrine signaling.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies (Goda et al., 2016; Mertens et al., 2005; Shafer et al., 2008).

claim: Andreani et al., 2022 showed a functional link between the clock and ER5 cells.
source: Andreani et al., 2022 also showed a functional link between the clock and ER5 cells, but the circuit mechanism was not elucidated.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Andreani et al., 2022.

claim: Links between clock output DN1 neurons to the ExR1 have been described.
source: Links between clock output DN1 neurons to the ExR1 have been described in Lamaze et al., 2018 and Guo et al., 2018, and Liang et al., 2019 described a connection from the clock to ExR2 (PPM3) dopaminergic neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies (Lamaze et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2018).

claim: Liang et al., 2019 described a connection from the clock to ExR2 (PPM3) dopaminergic neurons.
source: Links between clock output DN1 neurons to the ExR1 have been described in Lamaze et al., 2018 and Guo et al., 2018, and Liang et al., 2019 described a connection from the clock to ExR2 (PPM3) dopaminergic neurons.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liang et al., 2019.

claim: More than half of the CX cell types examined expressed a neuropeptide.
source: First, more than half of the cell types assayed express a neuropeptide.
evidence: This is supported by the data summarized in Figure 9.

claim: The fraction of cells expressing a neuropeptide appears to be several fold higher in the CX than in the adult brain as a whole.
source: This frequency is perhaps not surprising given that the CX is considered one of the most peptidergic regions of the adult brain (Kahsai and Winther, 2011; Nässel, 2018); nevertheless, the fraction of cells expressing an NP appears to be several fold higher in the CX than observed in the adult brain as a whole, as judged by single-cell RNA profiling studies (Davie et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of the authors' data with single-cell RNA profiling studies (Davie et al., 2018).

claim: The co-transmitter in neuropeptide-expressing CX cells was most often acetylcholine or glutamate.
source: This co-transmitter was most often acetylcholine or glutamate, but we observed cases of GABA, dopamine, tyramine, octopamine, and serotonin.
evidence: This is supported by the data summarized in Figure 9.

claim: The authors observed cases of GABA, dopamine, tyramine, octopamine, and serotonin as co-transmitters with neuropeptides in CX cells.
source: This co-transmitter was most often acetylcholine or glutamate, but we observed cases of GABA, dopamine, tyramine, octopamine, and serotonin.
evidence: This is supported by the data summarized in Figure 9.

claim: Neuropeptides fell into two broad categories based on expression patterns.
source: The neuropeptide expression patterns we observed fell into two broad categories.
evidence: This is a summary of the EASI-FISH data shown in Figures 5-7.

claim: Some neuropeptides appeared to be highly expressed in only a few relatively larger cells.
source: Some neuropeptides, like those whose expression patterns are shown in Figure 5, appeared to be highly expressed in only a few relatively larger cells.
evidence: This is supported by EASI-FISH data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Large neurosecretory cells often express the transcription factor DIMM.
source: Such large neurosecretory cells often express the transcription factor DIMM (Park et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Park et al., 2008.

claim: SIFa is expressed in broadly arborizing neurons that appear to deliver it to large areas of the brain and ventral nerve cord.
source: Several of these neuropeptides—for example, SIFa (Terhzaz et al., 2007) and Dsk (Wu et al., 2020)—are expressed in broadly arborizing neurons that appear to deliver them to large areas of the brain and ventral nerve cord.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies (Terhzaz et al., 2007) and the authors' EASI-FISH data.

claim: Dsk is expressed in broadly arborizing neurons that appear to deliver it to large areas of the brain and ventral nerve cord.
source: Several of these neuropeptides—for example, SIFa (Terhzaz et al., 2007) and Dsk (Wu et al., 2020)—are expressed in broadly arborizing neurons that appear to deliver them to large areas of the brain and ventral nerve cord.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies (Wu et al., 2020) and the authors' EASI-FISH data.

claim: Some neuropeptides are expressed in dozens to hundreds of cells and appear poised to function by transmission to nearby cells in multiple distinct circuits.
source: In contrast, neuropeptides like those shown in Figure 6 are expressed in dozens to hundreds of cells and appear poised to function by transmission to nearby cells in multiple distinct circuits.
evidence: This is supported by EASI-FISH data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Most of the neuropeptides shown in Figure 6 are expressed in the CX, each in distinct subsets of cell types.
source: As we show below, most of the neuropeptides shown in Figure 6 are expressed in the CX, each in distinct subsets of cell types.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figures 6, 8, and 9.

claim: In cases where more than one receptor has been identified for a given neuropeptide, the different receptors have distinct, but overlapping, expression patterns.
source: In cases where more than one receptor has been identified for a given neuropeptide, such as Dh44 (Figure 7G; reviewed in Lee et al., 2023) and Tk (Figure 7T; see Wohl et al., 2023), the different receptors have distinct, but overlapping, expression pattens.
evidence: This is supported by EASI-FISH data shown in Figure 7 and citations to published studies (Lee et al., 2023; Wohl et al., 2023).

claim: The authors used EASI-FISH to determine the expression patterns of 41 neuropeptides and 18 neuropeptide receptors in the adult central brain of females.
source: We used EASI-FISH to determine the expression patterns of these genes in the adult central brain of females (Figures 5—7). The list of 41 neuropeptides and 18 neuropeptide receptors we explored is presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach and is supported by the data shown in Figures 5-7 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The authors took a curated list of 51 neuropeptide-encoding genes from FlyBase and eliminated 12 genes based on their not having been detected in RNA profiling studies of the adult brain.
source: To look for expression of neuropeptides in the CX, we took a curated list of 51 neuropeptide-encoding genes from FlyBase (FB2024_02, released April 23, 2024; Öztürk-Çolak et al., 2024) and eliminated 12 genes based on their not having been detected in RNA profiling studies of the adult brain.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach with citation to FlyBase (Öztürk-Çolak et al., 2024).

claim: Trissin and Natalisin were added to the FlyBase list based on evidence summarized in Nässel, 2018.
source: Trissin and Natalisin were added to the FlyBase list based on evidence summarized in Nässel, 2018.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach with citation to Nässel, 2018.

claim: The authors selected 17 neuropeptides whose transcripts were observed in cell bodies located in the same general brain areas as those of the intrinsic cells of the CX.
source: We selected 17 neuropeptides whose transcripts were observed in cell bodies located in the same general brain areas as those of the intrinsic cells of the CX (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach.

claim: The authors characterized six CX cell types by RNA profiling.
source: We also characterized six CX cell types by RNA profiling (Figure 9—figure supplements 1 and 2) and additional RNA profiling of CX cell types is provided in Epiney et al., 2025.
evidence: This is supported by RNA profiling data shown in Figure 9—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: RNA profiling results are largely congruent with the EASI-FISH data.
source: These RNA profiling results are largely congruent with the EASI-FISH data and allow a comparison of transcript number and in situ signal strength.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of RNA profiling data (Figure 9—figure supplements 1 and 2) with EASI-FISH data (Figure 9).

claim: The authors used three metrics to assess sleep: sleep duration, P(Doze), and P(Wake).
source: As described in methods, we used three metrics: sleep duration; P(Doze), the probability that an active fly will stop moving; and P(Wake), the probability that a stationary fly will start moving.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach.

claim: The authors assayed multiple independent driver lines for most cell types identified as affecting sleep.
source: In most of these cases, we were able to assay multiple independent driver lines for the cell type.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach.

claim: Many lines showed phenotypes that differed between sexes, even though the expression patterns of the split-GAL4 lines did not obviously differ across sexes.
source: We observed that many lines showed phenotypes that differed between sexes, even though the expression patterns of the split-GAL4 lines did not obviously differ across sexes.
evidence: This is an observation based on the sleep assay data shown in Figures 10-11 and supplements.

claim: Lines that showed strong effects generally did so with both activation modes and with both beam crossing-based activity measures and video-based locomotion tracking.
source: Lines that showed strong effects generally did so with both activation modes and with both beam crossing-based activity measures and video-based locomotion tracking.
evidence: This is an observation based on the sleep assay data shown in Figures 10-11 and supplements.

claim: The connectome reveals that many of the intrinsic CX cell types with sleep phenotypes are connected by wired pathways.
source: Not surprisingly, the connectome reveals that many of the intrinsic CX cell types with sleep phenotypes are connected by wired pathways.
evidence: This is supported by connectivity data shown in Figure 12 and Figure 12—figure supplement 1.

claim: The strongest connections between CX cell types with sleep phenotypes are diagrammed in Figure 12.
source: The strongest of these connections are diagrammed in Figure 12, with Figure 12—figure supplement 1 also showing additional weaker connections.
evidence: This is supported by connectivity data shown in Figure 12.

claim: Activation of hDeltaF does not increase activity measures, showing that observed changes are not attributable to hyperactivity.
source: In addition to sleep duration and P(Wake) we also measured activity by beam counts/waking minute in the DAM assays and pixel movements/waking minute in video tracking. We found that activation of hDeltaF does not increase these measures, showing that observed changes are not attributable to hyperactivity (see Supplementary file 3, Supplementary file 4, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by activity data shown in Supplementary files 3, 4, and 5.

claim: Hamid et al., 2024 demonstrated expression of Tk in ventral FB neurons likely to correspond to the cell type shown in panel E of Figure 8.
source: Hamid et al., 2024 demonstrated expression of Tk in ventral FB neurons likely to correspond to the cell type shown in panel E.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hamid et al., 2024.

claim: Methods for using machine learning to predict neurotransmitter from EM images show great promise.
source: Methods for using machine learning to predict neurotransmitter from EM images show great promise (Eckstein et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Eckstein et al., 2024.

claim: Machine learning methods are unlikely to fully replace the need for experimental determination and validation of neurotransmitters.
source: However, they are unlikely to fully replace the need for experimental determination and validation for three reasons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' assessment of current machine learning capabilities.

claim: Rarely used transmitters such as tyramine are problematic for machine learning prediction due to limited training data.
source: First, rarely used transmitters such as tyramine are problematic due to limited training data.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' understanding of machine learning limitations.

claim: Accurate prediction of co-transmission is challenging for current computational approaches.
source: Second, accurate prediction of co-transmission is challenging for current computational approaches.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' understanding of machine learning limitations.

claim: FISH remains the gold standard for inferring gene expression.
source: Third, FISH remains the gold standard for inferring gene expression.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Neuropeptides provide a parallel mode of communication to wired connections and can act over larger distances using volume transmission.
source: Neuropeptides provide a parallel mode of communication to wired connections and can act over larger distances using volume transmission (reviewed in Nässel, 2009; Bargmann and Marder, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles (Nässel, 2009; Bargmann and Marder, 2013).

claim: Neuropeptides are widely expressed in the CX.
source: Neuropeptides are widely expressed in the CX (Kahsai and Winther, 2011; Nässel, 2018) and are likely to play important roles in its function.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies (Kahsai and Winther, 2011; Nässel, 2018).

claim: Information on the expression of neuropeptides and their receptors is not provided by the connectome.
source: However, information on the expression of neuropeptides and their receptors is not provided by the connectome.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of connectome data.

claim: Sleep is defined as 5 min or more of inactivity.
source: Sleep duration was defined as 5 min or more of inactivity (Hendricks et al., 2000; Shaw et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a standard definition in the field supported by citations to Hendricks et al., 2000 and Shaw et al., 2000.

claim: The authors did not examine the effects of inhibiting the function of cell types identified in the sleep screen.
source: For example, we did not examine the effects of inhibiting their function.
evidence: This is a statement about what experiments were not performed.

claim: The authors did not examine parameters such as arousal thresholds or recovery from sleep deprivation.
source: Nor did we examine parameters such as arousal thresholds or recovery from sleep deprivation.
evidence: This is a statement about what experiments were not performed.

claim: By using only a 24-hr activation protocol the authors might have missed features only observable in shorter activation protocols.
source: Finally, by using only a 24-hr activation protocol we might have missed features only observable in shorter activation protocols.
evidence: This is speculation about potential limitations of the experimental approach.

claim: The authors assayed all lines in both males and females with identical genetic and environmental manipulations.
source: On the other hand, we assayed all lines in both males and females with identical genetic and environmental manipulations and many lines were evaluated by both optogenetic and thermogenetic activation.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach.

claim: Many lines were evaluated by both optogenetic and thermogenetic activation.
source: On the other hand, we assayed all lines in both males and females with identical genetic and environmental manipulations and many lines were evaluated by both optogenetic and thermogenetic activation.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach.

claim: PEN_b is comprised of 22 columnar neurons linking the ellipsoid body (EB), protocerebral bridge (PB), and noduli.
source: PEN_b is comprised of 22 columnar neurons linking the ellipsoid body (EB), protocerebral bridge (PB), and noduli (Wolff and Rubin, 2018; Turner-Evans and Jayaraman, 2016 ; Green et al., 2017; Hulse et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies (Wolff and Rubin, 2018; Turner-Evans and Jayaraman, 2016; Green et al., 2017; Hulse et al., 2021).

claim: Thermogenetic activation of PEN_b using split-GAL4 lines SS02232 and SS54295 decreases sleep duration and increases P(Wake) in males.
source: Specifically, thermogenetic activation of these split-GAL4 lines decreases sleep duration and increases P(Wake) in males but only SS02232 is wake promoting in females.
evidence: This is supported by thermogenetic activation data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only SS02232 is wake promoting in females for PEN_b.
source: Specifically, thermogenetic activation of these split-GAL4 lines decreases sleep duration and increases P(Wake) in males but only SS02232 is wake promoting in females.
evidence: This is supported by thermogenetic activation data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: Optogenetic activation of SS02232 suppresses sleep and increases P(Wake) in both males and females supporting the general function of these neurons as wake promoting.
source: Optogenetic activation of SS02232 suppresses sleep and increases P(Wake) in both males and females supporting the general function of these neurons as wake promoting.
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic activation data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: SS54295 has stochastic expression that might explain the weaker wake promoting effect seen with this line.
source: While both lines show high cell type specificity and minimal VNC expression, SS54295 has stochastic expression that might explain the weaker wake promoting effect seen with this line.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed expression pattern and behavioral data.

claim: Thermogenetic and optogenetic activation of PFGs reveals sexually dimorphic sleep behavior.
source: Thermogenetic (A) and optogenetic (B) activation of PFGs reveals sexually dimorphic sleep behavior.
evidence: This is supported by thermogenetic and optogenetic activation data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 2.

claim: The authors tested four different split-GAL4 lines for PFGs.
source: We tested four different split-GAL4 lines for this cell type.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 2.

claim: All four PFG lines display expression in the VNC complicating interpretation of the results.
source: All four lines display expression in the VNC complicating interpretation of the results.
evidence: This is an observation based on the expression patterns shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 2.

claim: Optogenetic activation in female flies showed increased sleep in all four PFG driver lines.
source: Optogenetic activation (Day 2) in female flies showed increased sleep in all four driver lines and a mild increase in sleep duration in one of lines for male flies (SS52547).
